title: Technical Q&A, senior software engineer, average answers

questions.text: A service has intermittent timeouts under load. How do you find the cause?
Monolith or microservices for a team of ten engineers?
How would you make a payment API safe to retry?
How does consensus work, and when do you need it?
How do you explain technical debt trade-offs to a product leader?
How would you shard a database that has outgrown one machine?

persona.pushback_style: asks why not the simpler option and changes a constraint

brief.curveball: The largest customer needs 99.99 percent uptime starting next month. What changes in the design?

turns.speaker: interviewer
turns.text: Hi Gareth, thanks for joining. I'm Elise, an engineering manager. This is a thirty minute technical conversation. I ask spoken questions, I will push on answers, and there is no coding.

turns.speaker: candidate
turns.text: Hi Elise, thanks. Sounds fine.

turns.speaker: interviewer
turns.text: How long have you been in your current role?

turns.speaker: candidate
turns.text: Six years in total as an engineer, and the last two as a tech lead for a team of seven.

turns.speaker: interviewer
turns.text: Good. I'll ask three or four questions about reliability and design, and then leave time for yours.

turns.speaker: interviewer
turns.text: A service has intermittent timeouts under load. How do you find the cause?

turns.speaker: candidate
turns.text: I would start with the metrics and logs to see when the timeouts happen. Then check CPU, memory and the database connections. Usually it is a slow dependency or a thread pool that is full. I would use tracing to see where the time goes. Then fix the bottleneck.

turns.speaker: interviewer
turns.text: Give me a specific time you did this, and what you found.

turns.speaker: candidate
turns.text: We had timeouts on an order service every evening. Traces showed requests waiting on the database connection pool, which was set to 10. We raised it to 50 and the timeouts stopped. I led the investigation with two other engineers.

turns.speaker: interviewer
turns.text: Monolith or microservices for a team of ten engineers?

turns.speaker: candidate
turns.text: Microservices, I think, because they let teams work independently and scale separately. Each service can use the best technology. It is also more resilient because one failure does not take everything down. Most big companies use them.

turns.speaker: interviewer
turns.text: Why not the simpler option? A monolith is easier to build and run.

turns.speaker: candidate
turns.text: That is true, a monolith is simpler at the start. At my company we split ours when we had twelve engineers, and deploys went from weekly to daily. But it took about three months and we hit new network failures. For ten engineers I would probably start modular and split later.

turns.speaker: interviewer
turns.text: Suppose your largest customer needs ninety nine point nine nine percent uptime starting next month. What changes?

turns.speaker: candidate
turns.text: We would add redundancy, so several instances in different zones, and a load balancer with health checks. We would set up monitoring and alerts and an on call rotation. And maybe do more testing before releases.

turns.speaker: interviewer
turns.text: How much downtime per year does that target allow?

turns.speaker: candidate
turns.text: I think about fifty minutes a year. So we could not rely on manual recovery, and every deploy needs to be safe. I guess we would also need to practice failovers and have good alerts.

turns.speaker: interviewer
turns.text: How would you make a payment API safe to retry?

turns.speaker: candidate
turns.text: With an idempotency key. The client sends a unique key with each request, and the server stores the key with the result. If the same key arrives again, it returns the stored result instead of charging twice. At my company we added this and duplicate charges fell from about 30 a month to zero. We keep keys for 24 hours.

turns.speaker: interviewer
turns.text: Thanks. What questions do you have for me?

turns.speaker: candidate
turns.text: How does your team handle on call load for senior engineers?

turns.speaker: interviewer
turns.text: Senior engineers join a one in six rotation, and a week on call is followed by a week without project meetings.

turns.speaker: interviewer
turns.text: That's our time. Thanks Gareth, the recruiter will contact you within a week.

turns.speaker: candidate
turns.text: Thank you, Elise.

notes: Average for senior: general first answers, specifics only after probes. The uptime curveball gets a generic list.
